draft.title: The Green Revolution
card: The Green Revolution was a big rise in grain harvests that began in the 1960s. It happened mainly in parts of Asia and Latin America.
Three changes drove it: high-yield seed varieties, chemical fertilisers and more irrigation. Together they let each hectare produce much more rice, wheat and maize.
Higher harvests meant more food for growing populations. Countries such as India grew far more wheat and rice than before.
It also brought costs. Heavy irrigation can overuse water, and fertilisers and constant cropping can damage the soil.
draft.remember: More grain from each hectare, with costs for water and soil.

a.q: Which change was part of the Green Revolution?
opts: Planting high-yield seeds with fertiliser and irrigation
Moving crop farming to areas of colder climate
Replacing grain crops with livestock farming
Growing crops only for local village markets
a.why: The Green Revolution raised grain yields by combining high-yield seeds, fertilisers and irrigation. Moving to colder climates is wrong because the extra food came from changing farming methods, not from changing where crops were grown.
a.clue: Think about what was added to each hectare of farmland.

b.q: A farming district in northern India used high-yield wheat, fertiliser and irrigation from bores. Harvests rose, but after many years the water table dropped. What does this show?
opts: The yield gains came with a cost, as water was overused
The new seeds failed to raise the harvest at all
Irrigation was not part of the Green Revolution
The soil gained nutrients, so less water was needed
b.why: Harvests rose, which fits the Green Revolution, but heavy irrigation drew down the water. This is one of its costs. The claim that the seeds failed is wrong because the harvests did rise.
b.clue: Look at what happened to both the harvest and the water.

a.best: Planting high-yield seeds with fertiliser and irrigation

b.best: The yield gains came with a cost, as water was overused
